demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Akua had always taken pride in her meticulous attention to detail as an architect. She spent years honing her craft, working on high-profile projects, and building a reputation for herself in the industry. But all of that changed one fateful day when she accidentally caused serious injury to a colleague on a construction site. The memory of the incident has haunted her ever since. The more Akua reflects on what happened, the more she becomes convinced that someone else would not have gotten into this situation (Self-Comparison). She feels isolated and set apart from others, as if she's living in a constant state of shame (Isolation). Her self-doubt has grown to the point where she barely recognizes herself anymore (Unrecognisable Self). These negative appraisals of herself have led Akua to develop maladaptive strategies to cope with her guilt. She's begun performing mental rituals, like counting steps or tapping her foot a certain number of times, in an attempt to prevent anything bad from happening again (Magical Prevention). When the rituals don't work, she resorts to self-blame rumination, dwelling on what she has done wrong and replaying the incident over and over in her mind. As Akua tries to make sense of her thoughts and emotions, she finds it difficult to deliberately recall the details of the incident (Hard to Recall Deliberately). When memories do surface, they're often accompanied by vivid sensory experiences – the taste of sweat on her lips, the sound of sirens blaring in the distance (Taste Vividness, Auditory Recall). These fragmented memories only serve to reinforce her negative appraisals of herself. She starts to wonder if she's truly capable of designing safe buildings or if she's just a menace waiting to happen. Akua's memories also trigger false alarms, making her react as if she's in danger even when there's no real threat (False Alarms). The sound of a car horn or the creaking of a floorboard is enough to startle her and send her heart racing. She becomes hypervigilant, constantly on the lookout for potential hazards that might not even exist. This state of heightened arousal makes it difficult for Akua to concentrate, and she finds herself struggling to focus on even the simplest tasks (Concentration). In an attempt to regain control, Akua resorts to downward comparison, reminding herself that things could have been worse (Downward Comparison). She tries to rationalize her way out of her guilt, but this only leads to more rumination and self-blame. Her mind becomes a vicious cycle of negative appraisals, maladaptive strategies, and fragmented memories. As time goes on, Akua's relationships with her colleagues and loved ones begin to suffer. They notice the change in her demeanor – the constant checking and rechecking, the hesitation to take on new projects. They try to reassure her that it was an accident, but Akua can't shake off the feeling of responsibility. She starts to withdraw from social interactions, fearing that others will discover her "true" nature. It's only when Akua's husband sits her down and expresses his concern about her increasingly reclusive behavior that she realizes she needs help. The incident has left her with a deep-seated fear of causing harm to others, and she's desperate to break free from this cycle of guilt and self-doubt. As she begins therapy, Akua hopes to learn new ways to cope with her memories and negative appraisals, and to slowly rebuild her sense of self-worth as an architect and a person.
